title: EMT Course Map
body:
Every chapter of a standard US EMT-Basic course, mapped to the Rounds modules and lessons that teach it. Chapter numbering follows AAOS *Emergency Care and Transportation of the Sick and Injured* 12th edition; Brady *Emergency Care* 14th edition covers the same ground in a slightly different order, and the National EMS Education Standard for each row is named in the last column.

Use it two ways: before class, read the listed lessons for the chapter your instructor assigned; after class, use the same lessons as the review pass.

## Section 1: Preparatory

| Chapter / Standard | Rounds module | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| 1. EMS Systems (Preparatory: EMS Systems) | EMS Operations | The EMS system and who lets you do what; New Jersey EMS: tiers, direction, and reporting; Community paramedicine and the evidence behind it |
| 2. Workforce Safety and Wellness (Preparatory: Workforce Safety) | EMS Operations | Scene safety, staging, and the hazards that hurt crews; Lifting and moving without destroying your back; Infection control, wellness, and reading the evidence; Fatigue, sleep, and lasting in this career |
| 2b. Stress and the body's response | How the Body Stays Alive | Adrenaline and cortisol: the stress response that hides shock; Sleep, shift work and the body |
| 3. Medical, Legal and Ethical Issues (Preparatory: Medical/Legal) | Communication and Documentation | Consent, capacity, refusal, and advance directives; Duty to act, negligence, and the words that follow you; HIPAA, privacy, and mandated reporting; Refusals that are not simple; HIPAA on the street: twelve verdicts; Negligence and consent: eight cases |
| 3b. DNR, POLST and end-of-life orders | Special Populations, Extrication and Terrorism | Bariatric patients, hospice, DNR and POLST |
| 4. Communications and Documentation | Communication and Documentation | The 30-second report: radio, MIST, and SBAR; Closed-loop communication and speaking up; The patient care report: writing what holds up; Talking to someone who is frightened; Family, bystanders, and de-escalation; Language access and cultural humility; A radio phrase library for five call types; Calling medical control and taking an order; The patient care report, start to finish |
| 5. Medical Terminology | Medical Terminology | How medical words are built; Core roots, part one; Core roots, part two; Prefixes; Suffixes; Directions and positions; Planes, cavities, quadrants and regions; The abbreviations you will actually hear; Dangerous abbreviations and the do-not-use list; plus the whole second-pass extension |
| 6. The Human Body (Anatomy and Physiology) | The Human Body and Lifespan Development | Topographic anatomy, planes and directional terms; The skeleton, bone by bone; Muscles, joints and how the body moves; Respiratory anatomy: from nose to alveolus; The heart, the named vessels and the blood; The nervous system, top to bottom; Skin, gut, kidneys, glands and reproductive organs |
| 6b. The Human Body, function-first companion | How the Body Stays Alive | The whole game: oxygen in, CO2 out; Perfusion: pump, pipes, fluid, air; The eleven systems and what each one is for; Two wires: sympathetic and parasympathetic; Acid and base without the chemistry class; Water in three places: compartments and dehydration |
| 7. Pathophysiology | The Human Body and Lifespan Development | Cells, metabolism and perfusion: the pathophysiology chapter; What hypoperfusion does to each system |
| 7b. Pathophysiology companion | How the Body Stays Alive | Homeostasis and compensation; Shock: one idea, four families; Cells to systems, and what organ failure means; Inflammation in plain words; When cells run out of fuel: lactate as the shock signal |
| 8. Life Span Development | The Human Body and Lifespan Development | Lifespan development: neonate through older adult |
| 8b. Life span companion | How the Body Stays Alive / Vital Signs | What changes with age, system by system; Normal ranges by age; Pediatric vitals: drilling the age bands cold |
| 9. Lifting and Moving Patients | EMS Operations | Lifting and moving without destroying your back |

## Section 2: Patient Assessment

| Chapter / Standard | Rounds module | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| 10. Patient Assessment (Assessment: all) | Patient Assessment | The first 30 seconds: scene size-up; Primary survey; Sick or not sick, and the transport decision; History: the story the patient tells you; Secondary assessment; Vitals, trends, and reassessment; Medical flow versus trauma flow; Hard cases: altered, unresponsive, and refusing |
| 10b. Assessment, second pass | Patient Assessment (extension) | Choosing the exam: ten complaints, ten answers; Assessment at the extremes of age; Found down with no story; Multi-system trauma: the first ten minutes; When the second set of vitals changes the plan; Difficult historians; Handing off an assessment; Passing the patient assessment station |
| 10c. Vital signs in detail | Vital Signs | Pulse; Respirations; Blood pressure; MAP, pulse pressure, orthostatics; Pulse oximetry and when it lies; Temperature and pain; AVPU, GCS and glucose; Normal ranges by age; Trends, shock index, and documenting vitals; plus the whole extension |

## Section 3: Airway, Pharmacology, Shock and Resuscitation

| Chapter / Standard | Rounds module | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| 11. Airway Management (Airway, Respiration and Ventilation) | Airway, Respiration and Ventilation | Ventilation, oxygenation, respiration; The airway top to bottom; Adequate or not: reading the breathing; Opening and clearing the airway; Airway adjuncts: the OPA and the NPA; Oxygen delivery devices and their numbers; Oxygen cylinders, safety and the duration math; Ventilating: the bag-valve mask and the rates; CPAP: pressure, not oxygen; Choking, difficult airways and working with ALS |
| 11b. Airway, second pass | Airway (extension) | Coaching CPAP; BiPAP, transport ventilators and patients already on support; Supraglottic airways; Waveform capnography at the BLS level; Tracheostomy emergencies and the DOPE check; Airways that close; Oxygen myths and the cost of too much; Airway during CPR and after ROSC |
| 12. Principles of Pharmacology | EMT Pharmacology | What a drug is and how it gets in; The six rights; Oxygen and oral glucose; Aspirin and nitroglycerin; Epinephrine for anaphylaxis; Naloxone and activated charcoal; Albuterol, CPAP, glucometry and expanded scope; Reading a medication list as a history; Medication math, calling for orders, and charting; plus the whole extension |
| 12b. Dose and drip arithmetic | Medication and Clinical Math | All ten lessons, units through mixed practice |
| 13. Shock (Shock and Resuscitation) | How the Body Stays Alive / Cardiology and Resuscitation / Trauma | Shock: one idea, four families; Shock from the cardiac side; Hemorrhagic shock and the cliff; What hypoperfusion does to each system (Body and Lifespan) |
| 14. BLS Resuscitation | Cardiology and Resuscitation | Cardiac arrest and high-quality CPR; The AED; ROSC, post-arrest care, and when to stop; Pediatric arrest and drowning; Hypothermic arrest; Termination of resuscitation and the family; The post-ROSC bundle, second pass |

## Section 4: Medical

| Chapter / Standard | Rounds module | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| 15. Medical Overview | Medical Emergencies | Respiratory emergencies: telling them apart (as the entry point); Medical flow versus trauma flow (Patient Assessment) |
| 16. Respiratory Emergencies | Medical Emergencies + Medical Emergencies by System | Respiratory emergencies: telling them apart; Sorting sudden shortness of breath: COPD, heart failure, and clots; The rest of the respiratory chapter: pneumonia, pertussis, croup, epiglottitis, cystic fibrosis |
| 17. Cardiovascular Emergencies | Cardiology and Resuscitation + Medical Emergencies by System | The pump and the plumbing; The electrical system; Acute coronary syndrome; Treating chest pain: aspirin, nitro and the clock; Heart failure and acute pulmonary edema; Hypertensive emergency, aortic dissection and syncope; Acquiring a 12-lead and recognizing STEMI; The heart attacks that do not look like heart attacks; Pacemakers, ICDs and the magnet; The LVAD patient; The rest of the cardiovascular chapter: pulmonary edema, hypertensive crisis, aneurysm and cardiogenic shock |
| 18. Neurologic Emergencies | Medical Emergencies | Stroke: time is brain; Seizures, syncope, and altered mental status; Stroke second pass: posterior circulation and the mimics; Seizures in special populations |
| 19. Gastrointestinal and Urologic Emergencies | Medical Emergencies by System | The acute abdomen: organs, referred pain and the exam; GI bleeding, obstruction and the belly that kills; Urologic emergencies: stones, infection, retention, dialysis and ostomies; plus Abdominal, GI, and aortic emergencies and Belly pain by age and by sex in Medical Emergencies |
| 20. Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies | Medical Emergencies by System | Endocrine beyond the basics: diabetes complications, thyroid and adrenal; Hematologic emergencies: sickle cell, hemophilia and the anticoagulated patient; plus Diabetic emergencies and Diabetes second pass in Medical Emergencies |
| 21. Immunologic Emergencies | Medical Emergencies by System | Allergy to anaphylaxis: epinephrine and the biphasic reaction; plus Allergic reaction and anaphylaxis in Medical Emergencies and Epinephrine in the hard cases in Pharmacology |
| 22. Toxicology | Medical Emergencies | Overdose: opioids, alcohol, and stimulants; Poisons, gases, and decontamination; Reading the toxidromes; Overdoses that kill differently; plus Naloxone in the populations that complicate it (Pharmacology) |
| 23. Psychiatric Emergencies | Medical Emergencies by System | Psychiatric emergencies, restraint and excited delirium; plus Behavioral calls, sepsis, dialysis, and sickle cell in Medical Emergencies |
| 24. Gynecologic Emergencies | Medical Emergencies by System | Gynecologic emergencies and sexual assault care |

## Section 5: Trauma

| Chapter / Standard | Rounds module | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| 25. Trauma Overview and kinematics | Trauma | Kinematics: reading the mechanism of injury; Crush, blast, eyes, and the trauma system |
| 26. Bleeding | Trauma | Stopping the bleeding: the hemorrhage ladder; Hemorrhagic shock and the cliff; Tourniquets second pass: conversion, myths, and TXA |
| 27. Soft-Tissue Injuries | Trauma | Musculoskeletal injury and splinting; Burns: depth, size, and the critical list; plus Wound and orthopaedic care in the ED track |
| 28. Face and Neck Injuries | Trauma / Airway | Head injury and the Glasgow Coma Scale; Airways that close: burns, anaphylaxis, facial trauma and the obese patient |
| 29. Head and Spine Injuries | Trauma | Head injury and the Glasgow Coma Scale; Spine injury and selective motion restriction; Geriatric trauma and the anticoagulated patient; Athletes, helmets, and equipment removal |
| 30. Chest Injuries | Trauma | Chest trauma; Penetrating wounds of the chest and abdomen |
| 31. Abdominal and Genitourinary Injuries | Trauma | Abdominal trauma, evisceration, and impaled objects; Penetrating wounds of the chest and abdomen; The pelvic binder, step by step |
| 32. Orthopaedic Injuries | Trauma | Musculoskeletal injury and splinting; Splints that go wrong: pulseless, open, and dislocated; plus Muscles, joints and how the body moves (Body and Lifespan) |
| 33. Environmental Emergencies | Medical Emergencies | Environmental emergencies; plus Hypothermic arrest: not dead until warm and dead (Cardiology) and the water and ice sections of Rescue awareness |

## Section 6: Special Patient Populations

| Chapter / Standard | Rounds module | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| 34. Obstetrics and Neonatal Care | OB, Pediatrics and Geriatrics | Pregnancy changes the rules; OB emergencies: bleeding, pain and seizures; Delivering a baby: the normal sequence; When delivery goes wrong; Newborn care, APGAR and neonatal resuscitation; After the baby: hemorrhage, rupture and preterm labor; Neonatal resuscitation minute by minute |
| 35. Pediatric Emergencies | OB, Pediatrics and Geriatrics | Sizing up a child: the PAT and the numbers; Pediatric emergencies you will actually see; Wheezing children; Stridor, tracheitis and the choking child; Pediatric shock and dehydration by the numbers; The febrile infant; Pediatric trauma; Children with special healthcare needs; plus Pediatric trauma: small bodies, different rules (Trauma) |
| 36. Geriatric Emergencies | OB, Pediatrics and Geriatrics | Geriatrics and patients with special challenges; Geriatric syndromes: the fall workup, delirium and the pill bottle; plus Geriatric trauma and the anticoagulated patient (Trauma) and the older-adult section of Lifespan development |
| 37. Patients With Special Challenges | Special Populations, Extrication and Terrorism | Developmental and intellectual disability, autism and how to communicate; Hearing, vision and speech impairment on a call; Technology-dependent patients: tracheostomies and home ventilators; Feeding tubes, central lines, VP shunts and ostomies; Bariatric patients, hospice, DNR and POLST; Abuse and neglect: children, elders and intimate partners |

## Section 7: EMS Operations

| Chapter / Standard | Rounds module | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| 38. Transport Operations | Special Populations, Extrication and Terrorism + EMS Operations | Transport operations in depth: checks, driving, air medical and landing zones; Ambulance operations, driving, and air medical; Ambulance crashes: the data and the rules |
| 39. Vehicle Extrication and Special Rescue | Special Populations, Extrication and Terrorism | Vehicle extrication: scene, stabilization, access and rapid extrication; Rescue awareness: water, ice, confined space, trench and wilderness; plus Extrication: your job and fire's job (EMS Operations) |
| 40. Incident Management and MCI | EMS Operations | Mass casualty incidents and the command system; START and JumpSTART triage; Second pass on MCI: SALT and hospital notification |
| 41. Terrorism Response and Disaster Management | Special Populations, Extrication and Terrorism | Terrorism, CBRNE and disaster response; plus Hazmat and WMD awareness and Decontamination and CBRNE recognition in depth (EMS Operations) |

## The exam itself

| What | Rounds module | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| NREMT cognitive exam | Passing the NREMT | How the cognitive exam actually works; How to read an NREMT question; The unbreakable priority order; the three most-missed-topic lessons; the five domain reviews; The thirty hardest question patterns |
| NREMT psychomotor and state skills | Passing the NREMT | The psychomotor exam and the skill stations; Minute-by-minute scripts for the two assessment stations; Passing the patient assessment station (Patient Assessment) |
| New Jersey certification | Passing the NREMT | New Jersey certification and staying certified; New Jersey EMS: tiers, direction, and reporting (EMS Operations) |

## A week-by-week order that matches most 150-hour courses

1. Weeks 1-2: chapters 1-5. Modules: EMS Operations (first two lessons), Communication and Documentation, Medical Terminology.
2. Weeks 2-3: chapters 6-9. Modules: The Human Body and Lifespan Development, How the Body Stays Alive.
3. Weeks 3-4: chapter 10. Modules: Patient Assessment, Vital Signs.
4. Weeks 4-5: chapters 11-12. Modules: Airway, EMT Pharmacology, Medication and Clinical Math.
5. Weeks 5-6: chapters 13-14 plus the cardiac chapter. Modules: Cardiology and Resuscitation.
6. Weeks 6-9: chapters 15-24. Modules: Medical Emergencies, then Medical Emergencies by System.
7. Weeks 9-12: chapters 25-33. Module: Trauma.
8. Weeks 12-13: chapters 34-37. Modules: OB, Pediatrics and Geriatrics, then Special Populations, Extrication and Terrorism (first six lessons).
9. Weeks 13-14: chapters 38-41. Modules: EMS Operations (rest), Special Populations (last four lessons).
10. Weeks 15-16: review. Module: Passing the NREMT, plus every module's quiz bank on shuffle.

> **Key:** Nothing in a standard EMT course is outside this table. If your instructor assigns a chapter you cannot find here, it is almost certainly a state or agency supplement rather than a National EMS Education Standard.

> **On the exam:** The NREMT cognitive exam does not test by chapter. It draws from five domains: Airway/Respiration/Ventilation, Cardiology and Resuscitation, Trauma, Medical/Obstetrics/Gynecology, and EMS Operations, with about 85 percent of items on adult patients and 15 percent on pediatrics. Use this map to learn the material and the domain reviews in Passing the NREMT to rehearse the test.
